items.explanation: Televised in 1954, the hearings showed McCarthy bullying witnesses with no evidence — his support collapsed and the Senate censured him.
options: A. Americans cared little about communism
B. Eisenhower would back McCarthy unconditionally
C. McCarthy had little proof for his charges
D. McCarthy's massive popularity

option_explanations.A: Americans cared a great deal about communism in the early 1950s — the Red Scare was at its height. The hearings did not prove indifference; they proved McCarthy lacked evidence.
option_explanations.B: Eisenhower did not back McCarthy unconditionally — he privately disliked him and eventually let the Senate move against him. The hearings did not prove unconditional presidential support.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings were televised, and they showed McCarthy bullying witnesses with no proof behind his charges — most famously when Joseph Welch asked, 'Have you no sense of decency?' His support collapsed and the Senate censured him.
option_explanations.D: The hearings did not prove McCarthy's massive popularity — they destroyed it. His approval fell sharply after the hearings, the opposite of massive popularity.

items.explanation: Kennan's containment meant holding the line against Soviet expansion everywhere — not rolling communism back, not nuking Moscow.
options: A. Dislodge Communist regimes wherever they existed
B. Hold firm against Communist expansion worldwide
C. Threaten atomic war against the USSR
D. Rely on Western European allies
items.stem: The policy of containment held that America should

option_explanations.A: Dislodging Communist regimes wherever they existed was 'rollback,' not containment. Containment accepted existing Communist states and sought to stop their spread, not to overthrow them.
option_explanations.B: Correct. George Kennan's containment policy held that America should hold firm against Communist expansion worldwide — stopping the spread of Soviet influence without trying to roll back communism where it already ruled.
option_explanations.C: Threatening atomic war against the USSR was 'massive retaliation,' a later Eisenhower doctrine — not containment. Containment was about political and economic pressure, not nuclear threats.
option_explanations.D: Relying on Western European allies was part of how containment was carried out (NATO, the Marshall Plan), but it was not what the policy held. Containment was a global doctrine of holding the line, not a doctrine of dependence on allies.

items.explanation: U.S. factories, investments, and trade across Latin America — plus the Monroe Doctrine tradition — made Washington treat any leftist movement there as a threat to American capital.
options: A. America had deep economic interests there
B. Truman and Eisenhower were close to Latin leaders
C. Moscow targeted the region especially
D. The CIA kept failing in Latin operations
items.stem: America was keen to stop Communist expansion in Latin America because

option_explanations.A: Correct. America had deep economic interests in Latin America — U.S. factories, investments, and trade across the region, plus the Monroe Doctrine tradition — which made Washington treat any leftist movement there as a threat to American capital.
option_explanations.B: Truman and Eisenhower were not personally close to Latin leaders — the relationship was about American economic and strategic interests, not personal ties.
option_explanations.C: Moscow did not especially target Latin America in this period — Soviet attention was focused on Europe and Asia. American alarm in Latin America was driven by U.S. interests there, not by unusual Soviet focus.
option_explanations.D: CIA operations in Latin America (like Guatemala in 1954) were mostly seen in Washington as successes, not failures. Operational record was not the reason for the policy — protecting American economic stakes was.

items.explanation: HUAC's Hollywood probe swept up 1930s Party members, wartime makers of pro-Soviet films, and the defiant Fifth-Amendment witnesses — the blacklist followed.
options: A. They had attended Party meetings in the 1930s
B. They had made pro-Soviet wartime films
C. They took the Fifth before the committee
D. All of the above
items.stem: When HUAC investigated Hollywood, it suspected writers and actors who

option_explanations.A: True and part of HUAC's net: the committee really did target people who had attended Communist Party meetings in the 1930s. This alone is correct but incomplete.
option_explanations.B: True and part of HUAC's net: the committee really did suspect makers of pro-Soviet wartime films (like Mission to Moscow). This alone is correct but incomplete.
option_explanations.C: True and part of HUAC's net: the committee really did target witnesses who took the Fifth Amendment — the Hollywood Ten went to prison for contempt. This alone is correct but incomplete.
option_explanations.D: Correct — all three. HUAC's Hollywood probe swept up 1930s Party members, wartime makers of pro-Soviet films, and the defiant Fifth-Amendment witnesses — and the blacklist followed.

items.explanation: Republicans hammered Democrats over 'losing' China, Hiss at Yalta, and wartime concessions — but Truman actually created the federal loyalty program, so they couldn't charge he ignored domestic communism.
options: A. China went Communist under Truman
B. Alger Hiss had advised FDR at Yalta
C. Truman set up no loyalty-check system
D. Wartime deals eased the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe
items.stem: Republicans called Democrats 'soft on communism' for all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: China going Communist under Truman really was a charge Republicans made — 'losing China' was their battle cry. This was a real charge, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Alger Hiss advising FDR at Yalta really was a charge — Republicans tied Democrats to Hiss's treason. This was a real charge, not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the exception. Truman actually created the federal loyalty-check system (Executive Order 9835, 1947), so Republicans could not charge that he had set up no loyalty program — he had been the one to build it.
option_explanations.D: Wartime deals easing the Soviet takeover of Eastern Europe really was a charge — Republicans blamed Yalta and wartime concessions. This was a real charge, not the exception.

items.explanation: Bentley tells HUAC the Silvermaster group supplied 'complete data as to almost all of the aircraft production in the country... how many were being produced, where they were allocated,' plus 'inside information on policies of the Air Corps' -- 'we knew D-Day long before D-Day happened.' The atomic spies were a different ring (the Rosenbergs); she names no HUAC members and says nothing of the Marshall Plan.
options: A. Detailed inside information on U.S. aircraft production and military plans, including D-Day
B. The design secrets of the atomic bomb
C. The identities of HUAC's own members
D. Advance plans for the Marshall Plan
items.stem: According to her testimony, Bentley's Soviet contacts had obtained
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Questioner: Can you describe the military information you obtained through the Silvermaster group? Bentley: I passed along classified material on aircraft production and other defense matters, gathered from government employees sympathetic to the Soviet cause.
—After Elizabeth Bentley's testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, 1948

option_explanations.A: Correct. Bentley tells HUAC the Silvermaster group supplied 'complete data as to almost all of the aircraft production in the country... how many were being produced, where they were allocated,' plus 'inside information on policies of the Air Corps' — 'we knew D-Day long before D-Day happened.'
option_explanations.B: The atomic bomb's design secrets came from a different spy ring — the Rosenbergs' network, not Bentley's Silvermaster group. She testified about aircraft production, not the Manhattan Project.
option_explanations.C: Bentley named no HUAC members as contacts — her testimony was about the Silvermaster group's government sources, not about the committee's own members.
option_explanations.D: The Marshall Plan came in 1947–48, after the wartime espionage Bentley described. Her testimony concerned wartime aircraft production and military plans, not the Marshall Plan.

items.explanation: Congress answered the spy revelations with internal-security legislation, above all the McCarran Internal Security Act of 1950 -- requiring communist organizations to register and tightening deportation and detention powers -- passed over Truman's veto. HUAC was not abolished, the FBI's powers grew rather than shrank, and the Smith Act stayed on the books.
options: A. it abolished the House Committee on Un-American Activities
B. it ended all federal loyalty investigations
C. it passed internal-security laws such as the McCarran Act
D. it sharply reduced the FBI's domestic powers
items.stem: Revelations of Soviet espionage like Bentley's led Congress to
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Questioner: Can you describe the military information you obtained through the Silvermaster group? Bentley: I passed along classified material on aircraft production and other defense matters, gathered from government employees sympathetic to the Soviet cause.
—After Elizabeth Bentley's testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, 1948

option_explanations.A: Congress did not abolish HUAC in response to the spy revelations — the committee continued its investigations for years afterward. Abolition was the opposite of Congress's response.
option_explanations.B: Congress did not end federal loyalty investigations — it intensified them. The response to the espionage revelations was more security machinery, not less.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Congress answered the spy revelations with internal-security legislation, above all the McCarran Internal Security Act of 1950 — requiring communist organizations to register and tightening deportation and detention powers — passed over Truman's veto.
option_explanations.D: Congress did not reduce the FBI's domestic powers — the Bureau's counterintelligence role grew during the Red Scare, not shrank.

items.explanation: Both were federal anti-radical campaigns driven by fear of revolution: Attorney General Palmer's 1919-1920 raids rounded up and deported thousands of suspected radicals in the First Red Scare, just as HUAC's hearings hunted suspected communists in the Second. The Whiskey prosecutions, Dred Scott, and Teapot Dome belong to entirely different stories.
options: A. The Whiskey Rebellion prosecutions of the 1790s
B. The Palmer Raids of 1919-1920
C. The Dred Scott decision
D. The Teapot Dome investigation
items.stem: HUAC's investigations most directly continued the precedent of

Questioner: Can you describe the military information you obtained through the Silvermaster group? Bentley: I passed along classified material on aircraft production and other defense matters, gathered from government employees sympathetic to the Soviet cause.
—After Elizabeth Bentley's testimony before the House Committee on Un-American Activities, 1948

option_explanations.A: The Whiskey Rebellion prosecutions were about tax resistance in the 1790s, not about hunting radicals for their beliefs. They belong to a different story entirely.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Both were federal anti-radical campaigns driven by fear of revolution: Attorney General Palmer's 1919–1920 raids rounded up and deported thousands of suspected radicals in the First Red Scare, just as HUAC's hearings hunted suspected communists in the Second.
option_explanations.C: The Dred Scott decision was about slavery and citizenship in 1857, not about investigating radicals. It belongs to an entirely different story.
option_explanations.D: The Teapot Dome investigation was about oil-lease corruption in the 1920s, not about anti-communism. It belongs to an entirely different story.
